title: Impact of Mass Deworming on School Attendance

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID).  
Why: We observe treated and control schools before and after program rollout.  The interaction term `treat_x_post` provides the causal contrast.  

Key identifying assumption: In the absence of the deworming program, treated and control schools would have displayed parallel trends in attendance (Parallel Trends Assumption).  We will probe this with (i) a placebo test using pre-periods only and (ii) a specification that allows unit-specific linear time trends.

## 2. R Code
```r
###############################
# Impact of Mass Deworming on School Attendance
# Difference-in-Differences implementation with robustness checks
###############################

# Load required libraries
required_pkgs <- c("data.table", "fixest", "sandwich", "lmtest")
new_pkgs <- required_pkgs[!(required_pkgs %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(new_pkgs)) install.packages(new_pkgs, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1. Read data --------------------------------------------------------------
file_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s49_data.csv"
dt <- fread(file_path)

# Ensure factors for fixed effects
dt[, unit_id := factor(unit_id)]
dt[, period  := factor(period)]

# 2. Baseline DID -----------------------------------------------------------
did_baseline <- feols(y ~ treated * post | unit_id + period, data = dt, cluster = "unit_id")

cat("Baseline DID result:\n")
print(coeftable(did_baseline)["treated:post", , drop = FALSE])

# 3. Robustness check 1: Unit-specific linear trends -----------------------
# Create numeric period for trend
dt[, t_numeric := as.numeric(as.character(period))]
did_trend <- feols(y ~ treated * post | unit_id + period + i(unit_id, t_numeric), data = dt, cluster = "unit_id")

cat("\nDID with unit-specific linear trends:\n")
print(coeftable(did_trend)["treated:post", , drop = FALSE])

# 4. Robustness check 2: Placebo test (pre-periods only) -------------------
pre_dt <- dt[post == 0]                      # keep only pre-program observations
# Artificially assign a placebo "post" in the middle of pre-periods
# (use the median pre period as cut)
median_pre <- median(as.numeric(as.character(pre_dt$period)))
pre_dt[, placebo_post := as.numeric(as.character(period)) > median_pre]
pre_dt[, treat_x_placebo := treated * placebo_post]

placebo_mod <- feols(y ~ treat_x_placebo | unit_id + period, data = pre_dt, cluster = "unit_id")

cat("\nPlacebo test within pre-periods:\n")
print(coeftable(placebo_mod)["treat_x_placebo", , drop = FALSE])
```

The script
1. Loads the data,
2. Estimates the baseline DID with school and period fixed effects, clustered at the school level,
3. Adds school-specific linear trends,
4. Runs a placebo DID restricted to pre-program observations to detect spurious effects.

The key causal estimate is the coefficient on `treated:post`.  

## 3. Expected Findings  
Because deworming is typically beneficial, a negative impact on attendance—if present—should be small.  I expect the coefficient on `treated:post` to be around −0.02 to −0.05 (i.e., a 2–5 percentage-point drop in attendance or roughly −0.15 to −0.30 standard-deviation units), and not statistically significant once trends are controlled for.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in attendance rates over time between treated and untreated schools.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The mass deworming program is associated with a decrease in school attendance rates.
